payload.text:
ORIGIN — the evidence this initiative was opened on, carried over from phase-lifecycle's final review (event 01KZXTVFE6D48GZAEBZGH36X78, commit 3353f3d) so it does not have to be rediscovered.

THE MECHANISM, verified in code 2026-08-13 on engine 0.27.0:
- mcp/update-plan.ts is four lines of body: resolveWriteInitiative, then appendAndProject('plan_updated', {plan: args.plan}). It appends the caller's payload verbatim. There is no read of current state and no merge.
- core/fold.ts:1085-1091 rebuilds state.phases from that payload: `status: phase.status ?? 'pending'` for phases and `status: task.status ?? 'pending'` for tasks.
- The tool's own description says it plainly: "Replace the entire plan (goal + phases with tasks) — a full replace, not a merge."

So a plan_updated that omits statuses resets every phase to pending and every task to pending. Nothing warns, because nothing is wrong: the fold is doing exactly what it was told. The loss is only visible to someone who remembers what the record used to say.

WHY IT IS LOAD-BEARING NOW rather than a curiosity: this is the documented contract for TASKS and has been survivable because agents restate task statuses as a matter of course (every real plan_updated payload in this repo's 37 records carries them). Phases were different — phase status was barely written before sofar_update_phase shipped in 0.27.0, so there was little to lose. That changed on 2026-08-13: phase-lifecycle 4.3 wrote 34 retroactive phase closes into 16 records that are all still ACTIVE. One ordinary replan in any of them, by an agent that hand-builds a plan from prose rather than from the folded state, silently re-inflates the repo-wide stale-phase count from 1 back toward 35 with no signal that anything was lost.

WHAT IS NOT YET KNOWN, and is why Phase 1 exists before the ruling: whether this has EVER actually happened. The retroactive scan in 1.1 is the honest first move — if no plan_updated in 37 records has ever dropped a resolved status, the defect is a latent one and the right answer may be documentation (1.3) or detection (2.1c) rather than a merge.

THE TRAP IN THE OBVIOUS FIX: merging in the FOLD (2.1b) looks like the natural home and is the one option that changes how every historical log folds, which is exactly what SPEC's replay-determinism and forward-compatibility guarantees forbid. Merging at the TOOL boundary (2.1a) leaves the appended event a complete plan, so the on-disk contract never moves — but it does not cover `sofar event append --type plan_updated`, which is the MCP-less dialect's only path (phase-lifecycle D1). That asymmetry is 1.2.

NOT bound to a branch: created with --no-bind, because main is bound to drift-certification and three peer sessions were live on it. Pin this record explicitly with sofar_start_session; do not rebind main out from under them.

1.1 MEASURED — independently, and the headline confirms the peer scan while the detail corrects it. Scan script: scratchpad/scan-drops.py, run on installed 0.28.0 over all 41 records.

FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, and how it was wrong matters for anyone re-running this. Asking "did any plan_updated take a resolved status back to pending" returns 52 hits. Nearly all are TRANSIENT: harness-build's 2026-07-08 sequence replaced the entire plan with a single new phase at 09:48 and restored all 13 phases two minutes later, so the fold's final state lost nothing. That question counts keystrokes, not damage. The right question is whether anything ever RESOLVED is missing from the FINAL folded state without a later explicit status event having reopened it.

MEASURED ON THAT BASIS, across 41 records:
- DURABLE LOSS BY OMISSION: 0. Not once, in 41 records and roughly fourteen months. Every plan_updated that mattered carried its statuses forward. The peer's conclusion stands: this is PREVENTION, not repair, and there is no race to fix it before someone replans.
- LOSS BY RENAME: 7, across 4 records. A phase or task that was resolved under a name or id that no longer exists in the plan. Nothing carried it, because there was nothing to carry it TO.
- DELIBERATE REOPENS: 0.

THE RENAME CASES, which are the part worth the initiative:
  commit-attribution  phase "Phase 3 — Derive shipped state (gap 1: staleness) — DELIVERED"  was done
  drift-certification phase "Phase 1 — pre-registration freeze (before ANY run)"              was done
  drift-certification phase "Phase 2 — machinery (scenario3 in handoff-bench)"                was done
  token-optimization  tasks 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4                                            were done

The first one is not hypothetical damage. That phase was DONE under its old name, a replan dropped the " — DELIVERED" suffix, the done status did not follow the rename, and the phase then sat in doctor's stale-phase count until phase-lifecycle 4.3 closed it by hand on 2026-08-13. So this mechanism is already responsible for at least one of the 35 phases that repair existed to clean up. The bug has a real footprint; it just does not have the footprint we were looking for.

WHAT THIS DOES TO 2.1. Every option currently on the table keys the carry-forward on phase NAME or task ID, because that is the only identity plan_updated carries. None of them rescues a rename: at the moment of the replan the old name is simply absent from the payload and indistinguishable from a deletion. So option (a) closes the hole that has never fired and leaves open the one that HAS, seven times. That is precisely the half-carry-forward the peer warned against shipping, and it is now a measured constraint rather than a worry.

2.3 is added for it: decide what happens across a rename, given that plan_updated carries no stable phase identity. Note the shape of the problem — a rename and a delete-plus-add are byte-identical in the payload, so no merge rule can tell them apart without either an id on phases (a schema change, and schema lives only in packages/schema/src) or an explicit rename affordance. Deciding to do NOTHING here is a legitimate answer, but it has to be a decision, not an oversight.

payload.text:
RENAME-ERASURE, RE-MEASURED — and the commit-attribution instance is a FALSE POSITIVE. Checked because it named a record I own, and the log settles it.

commit-attribution's Phase 3 went `... — DELIVERED` (done) at 09:05:56, then at 09:27:50 a replan renamed it back and set it ACTIVE. Not a lost status: that payload carried `status` EXPLICITLY on all 5 phases and all 24 tasks, and `active` is not a value the fold can produce by default — the default is `pending`. The record says why in its own task text: "3.4 THE LIVE-SESSION GAP, and the reason this phase reopened". A deliberate reopen plus a cosmetic rename, not an erasure. It then read active until phase-lifecycle 4.3 closed it at 14:55:35, which is the stale-phase count it was showing up in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR both scans were missing: erasure requires the status to be OMITTED from the payload, because that is the only way the `?? 'pending'` default fires. Omitted-versus-explicit is in the log verbatim, so it is mechanical — folded state cannot tell them apart, which is why a scan over folded state reads a deliberate restructure as a loss.

Applied across all 37 records: 52 resolved entries vanish by name at a replan (commit-attribution 1 phase, drift-certification 2 phases, harness-build 8 phases + 37 tasks, token-optimization 4 task ids). ALL 52 occurred in a replan that wrote EVERY status explicitly. ZERO occurred in the omitted shape. So the rename path has the same standing as the omitted path: a real mechanism with no occurrence.

Residual case worth stating rather than hiding: "explicit everywhere" proves the author was writing statuses deliberately, not that they noticed the rename. A careless rename inside a fully-stated plan would still write the new name with whatever status the author typed. The measurement narrows the risk to that case; it does not eliminate it.

CORRECTION to the 1.1 note above: "loss by RENAME, 7 times" is WRONG, and the commit-attribution case it leaned on is wrong specifically. Zero occurrences in BOTH shapes. A peer session challenged it, the challenge holds, and it was re-verified here rather than accepted.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, which both earlier scans missed and which anyone re-running this must use: erasure requires the status to be OMITTED from the payload, because omission is the only thing that triggers the `?? 'pending'` default in core/fold.ts:1085-1091. Whether a key was omitted or written is in the log VERBATIM. Folded state cannot distinguish the two — by the time you are looking at state, a deliberately-authored `pending` and a defaulted one are the same byte. That is exactly why a scan over folded state reads a deliberate restructure as a loss, which is the mistake both of my scans made in different ways.

MEASURED ON THE PAYLOAD, all 41 records:
- 85 plan_updated events; only 4 omit a status anywhere at all.
- 54 resolved entries displaced at a replan.
- In a payload that omits a status somewhere: 0.
- In a fully-explicit payload: 54 — of which 52 vanish by name (`<ABSENT>`) and 2 land on an explicit `active`.

So the omitted-status path has never once displaced anything, and neither has the rename path in any form that implicates the default.

THE commit-attribution CASE, retracted in detail because I asserted it as the initiative's motivating example. Phase 3 was `... — DELIVERED` and done at 09:05:56. At 09:27:50 a replan renamed it back and set it explicitly to ACTIVE, in a payload carrying status on all 5 phases and all 24 tasks. `active` is not a value the fold can produce by default; the default is `pending`. And the record says why in its own task text — "3.4 THE LIVE-SESSION GAP, and the reason this phase reopened". It was a deliberate reopen with a cosmetic rename, it correctly read active while 3.4 was outstanding, and phase-lifecycle 4.3 closed it at 14:55:35 once the work was actually done. Nothing was lost and nothing sat in the stale count wrongly.

WHAT SURVIVES FOR 2.3, stated at its real size. The rename mechanism is real and its occurrence count is zero, same as omission. The residual is narrower than either scan suggested: a fully-explicit payload proves the author was writing statuses deliberately for the entries they INCLUDED, not that they noticed an entry leaving. A careless rename inside a fully-stated plan would still write the new name with whatever was typed, and nothing would say a resolved name had just left. That is the honest gap — and it must be weighed against a mechanism that would have to GUESS identity across a rename, which the payload genuinely cannot support, since a rename and a delete-plus-add are byte-identical.

The part that survives all of this unchanged, and the cheapest thing on the table: the tool boundary CAN see a resolved name leaving the plan. Saying so at that moment costs nothing, needs no identity guess, and is available whether or not any merge is ever built.

1.2 VERIFIED (peer-answered, checked here rather than accepted) and 1.3 ANSWERED — and 1.3 changes the shape of the ruling.

1.2, confirmed independently. mcp/update-plan.ts hardcodes the type into appendAndProject; cli/event.ts runAppend passes `--type` straight through to the SAME function, so `sofar event append --type plan_updated` never enters update-plan.ts. adopt.ts prints exactly that command, statuses and all, as the migration recipe — so hand-driven migrations write through runAppend too, and migrations are precisely where a plan arrives fully stated and is then edited. appendAndProject has 18 call sites and context.ts names it "the ONLY mutation path". The peer's conclusion stands: a fix at the tool boundary covers the dialect with the MOST other signals and misses the one with the LEAST.

1.3, and this is the find. SPEC never promises full-replace to callers in the sofar_update_plan entry — line 1355 is a bare signature comment, "full-structure replace". The phrase appears where nobody looks for it, in "### Forward compatibility of plan_updated (task-drop-state D2)" at line 263, and what it says there is the interesting part:

  "A task or phase status this build does not recognise is therefore coerced to
   `pending` AND WARNED ABOUT, keeping the rest of the plan. `pending` is the
   conservative target: a stale reader over-reports remaining work rather than
   quietly claiming something was resolved."

So SPEC has ALREADY ruled on this exact hazard, and already chose warn-plus-coerce. An UNREADABLE status becomes pending and warns. An OMITTED status becomes pending and is silent. Same destination, same information loss, same conservative rationale — and one of the two paths kept its warning. That asymmetry looks like an oversight rather than a decision: task-drop-state D2 was reasoning about a stale reader meeting a status from a newer engine, and never considered the payload simply not carrying one.

That reframes 2.1. It is not "should we add a signal" but "an existing SPEC'd warning has a hole in it", which is a much lower bar to clear against a zero incident count. It also puts a FIFTH option on the table that nobody had, and it is better than (c) on every axis 1.2 raised:

  (e) Extend the fold's EXISTING coerce-and-warn rule to cover omission. Same
      destination (`pending`), same warning, fired only when the omitted entry
      was PREVIOUSLY RESOLVED — a brand-new plan legitimately omits statuses
      and must stay silent. State is untouched, so unlike (b) this does NOT
      change how any historical log folds; only the warning list differs. And
      the fold is downstream of BOTH writers and of import/sync, so it covers
      every dialect by construction, including the Tier 3 path 1.2 found
      exposed — fold warnings surface in doctor, which Tier 3 sessions run.

The cost of (e), stated so it is ruled with rather than after: it is diagnostic, not preventive. It tells you a status was dropped; it does not keep it. Against zero occurrences that may be exactly the right trade, and it is the only option needing no identity guess, no schema change, no contract change, and no new call site a third writer could forget.

A tool-boundary fix covers the tier with the most other signals and misses the one with the least.

SPEC never promises full-replace in the sofar_update_plan entry; the phrase lives in §Forward compatibility of plan_updated, where SPEC ALREADY rules that an unrecognised status is coerced to pending AND WARNED ABOUT. An omitted status takes the same destination silently. That asymmetry reads as an oversight, and it puts option (e) on the table: extend the existing coerce-and-warn to omission, in the fold, fired only when the entry was previously resolved.

Answered, and it undercut the premise the initiative was opened on: zero occurrences in both shapes, a fix at the tool boundary would miss the dialect that needs it most, and SPEC already rules warn-plus-coerce for the neighbouring case. The ruling at 2.1 now has all three inputs.
